# Choose the first-version provider and rollout contract

## Question

Which providers and operating systems must the first usable Chartr memory release support, and what must work in the manual-memory stage versus the automatic-extraction stage? Define observable cross-provider continuity scenarios, what happens for unsupported/custom agents, and whether already-running sessions must gain memory access. The agreed destination includes both stages; this decision fixes their acceptance boundary without treating every provider as equally capable.

Options for discussion (not decisions):

- Start with a small named provider set and expand through capability-based adapters
- Require manual memory for every MCP-capable Chartr provider, with automatic capture for a named subset
- Require manual memory and automatic capture for every currently supported Chartr provider

## Done when

The human selects the initial provider/OS matrix, stage gates, unsupported-provider behavior, and concrete success scenarios.

## Answer

Resolved with the operator on 2026-09-26.

### Required support and deployment

- Chartr clients target macOS and Linux. Native Windows Chartr support is deferred.
- Codex, Claude Code, and Grok Build are the required providers for explicit memory access and automatic capture. OpenCode remains researched but is not a required first-version provider.
- Use the operator's same existing Windows-hosted SurrealDB instance and its stored history. The verified development connection is `ws://127.0.0.1:8000`, namespace `harness`, database `memory`; this is not yet a reachable macOS/Linux deployment endpoint. The runtime decision must supply the remote connection and access boundary. No database rebind, provisioning, or credential changes were performed here.
- This remains one operator using one database instance. The earlier single-machine restriction is superseded because the operator explicitly requires macOS/Linux clients to use the Windows-hosted instance. Multi-user tenancy and database replication remain out of scope.
- Existing database history must be accessible according to the selected scope, lifecycle, and compatibility rules. Separate ingestion of old provider transcript files is not required. [Define compatibility with existing SurrealDB history](13-existing-surrealdb-history.md) owns the detailed mapping and coexistence contract.

### Rollout and acceptance

1. **Explicit-memory stage:** independently usable before automatic capture is ready. Each required provider must be able to write through the memory tools and retrieve eligible existing history. Verify cross-provider retrieval in fresh sessions after restart, visible provenance, and exclusion of unrelated project memory. Cover all six directed provider pairings on each target OS against the shared Windows-hosted instance.
2. **Automatic-capture stage:** may roll out provider by provider, but is complete only when all three required providers pass on macOS and Linux. Completed new work produces attributable typed memory under the agreed authority rules; another provider can retrieve eligible results; interruption/replay does not create duplicate memories; and skipped or failed capture is visible. Existing database history remains accessible alongside newly captured knowledge. This does not authorize automatic activation of hard rules; that policy belongs to the lifecycle ticket.
3. **Compatibility evidence:** use a declared compatibility contract and report inaccessible or unsupported history rather than silently claiming complete access. Provider capabilities documented in research are not a tested version matrix. Runtime acceptance must name the tested provider releases and existing database/schema compatibility. Exact adapters, extraction mechanisms, scope matching, retry rules, and budgets remain in their responsible tickets.

### Session and fallback behavior

- Access is guaranteed for supported newly started or explicitly resumed sessions after configuration; restart/resume may be required where a provider cannot reload. Seamless upgrade of every already-running session is not a requirement.
- Unsupported/custom agents remain usable as terminals. Show whether memory is available, unavailable, or unverified. Explicitly configured MCP access may be used without a full support guarantee; memory support is not a prerequisite for launching an unsupported agent.

### Evidence and boundaries

[Provider capability research](01-provider-memory-capabilities.md) and [Grok capability research](11-grok-memory-capabilities.md) establish candidate public interfaces. [Existing-instance evidence](../assets/existing-instance-context.md) establishes the current service/configuration, not its schema or remote reachability. Detailed database compatibility and network/runtime decisions remain open. The operator's stored-history clarification rules the separate provider-import ticket out of scope.

# Define memory scope and provenance identities

## Question

How should one operator's memory identify projects, repositories, worktrees, folder spaces, Free sessions, agents, and source runs across macOS/Linux clients using the existing Windows-hosted database? Decide the sharing and filtering rules across renamed directories, identical basenames, multiple clones, worktree-specific facts, global preferences, and private/work knowledge. Replace the draft's T3 thread/turn assumptions with explicit provenance requirements; preserve original-provider evidence pointers even when Chartr closes. Define identity collision handling and which trusted component supplies scope.

Options for discussion (not decisions):

- Repository identity with explicit workspace/worktree overrides and operator-global scope
- Chartr folder-space identity with explicit links between spaces
- An explicit memory-project identity independent of folders and repositories

## Done when

Canonical terms, stable identifiers, provenance fields, and a worked scope/filter matrix cover same-basename repos, clones, worktrees, Free sessions, and global/private records.

## Answer

Resolved with the operator on 2026-09-26. The operator selected the recommended choices in all three rounds and confirmed the final proposed contract. [Discussion history](../assets/scope-identity-discussion.md) retains the questions and alternatives; this Answer is the canonical resolution.

### Stable identity and project membership

A memory project is independent of a directory, Chartr folder space, repository remote, and provider. It can explicitly contain several repositories and non-git folders. Its knowledge is shared across the operator's macOS/Linux clients using the existing Windows-hosted database, subject to the binding and restrictions below.

| Identity | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| Memory project | Stable opaque identity; title, slug, and directory basename are not identity. |
| Repository | Stable opaque identity registered with repository aliases. Normalized remotes help identify a registered repository; they are not its sole durable identity. |
| Client installation | Stable opaque identity distinguishing source installations even when paths and native provider IDs coincide. Duplicate installation registrations require reconciliation, not silent merging. |
| Checkout/worktree | Stable opaque identity for one registered checkout. New clones/worktrees receive distinct identities and may share the same repository/project. |
| Folder space | Chartr's UI ownership/location concept, explicitly linked to memory identity; it does not define memory identity. |
| Conversation | Stable opaque identity linked to installation-qualified provider/native-session evidence when verified. A provisional local conversation is allowed before verification. |
| Source run | Stable service-assigned identity attributing a memory write or capture unit to its originating work. Capture-unit granularity and replay rules belong to the capture contract. |
| Agent | Provider plus conversation/source-run context, with role and model when known. A model name or transient terminal ID does not identify durable source work. |

An unambiguous previously registered repository match automatically selects its memory project only within the operator-selected work/personal boundary. Multiple candidate projects, conflicting aliases, forks, and ambiguous matches require explicit linking. Basenames and paths alone never merge projects. A verified move/rename preserves registration and identity; if continuity cannot be verified, ask to relink. Identical knowledge slugs in different projects or boundaries remain distinct. Within-scope write conflicts and exact record keys belong to the lifecycle/tool contracts.

Project-wide knowledge is shared across linked repositories and worktrees. Repository-qualified knowledge remains qualified to its repository; worktree-specific facts remain local to that checkout unless deliberately shared or generalized. Non-git folders can be linked explicitly without inventing a repository identity.

### Memory binding and authority

The operator selects a session's memory binding: work/personal boundary, optional memory project, applicable repository and checkout/worktree, conversation, and private-access permission. Chartr supplies this binding through trusted integration; the memory service enforces it on reads, writes, bootstrap, search, direct record lookup, graph traversal, and evidence access. Agent-supplied parameters may narrow access but cannot authorize another project or boundary. Authentication and transport mechanisms belong to the runtime ticket.

Work and personal knowledge are separate. Eligible operator-wide preferences accompany project knowledge by default within their allowed boundary; the caller may exclude them. A preference explicitly marked safe for both can be available in both. Global scope never bypasses private, repository, worktree, or session restrictions.

Private is an additional opt-in restriction within either work or personal, not a synonym for personal. Private content is excluded on every access path until the operator enables private access for the binding. Unknown/unmapped scope or sensitivity is not inferred to be global or normal. Existing-history mappings remain owned by the compatibility ticket.

A Free session has no memory project. After selecting its work/personal boundary it receives eligible global preferences, while other new knowledge stays local to that conversation until explicitly assigned or published. Its cwd does not supply a project implicitly.

Changing cwd or moving a UI pane never changes memory authority. Switching memory project or work/personal boundary starts a fresh provider conversation: already-retrieved context cannot be removed by changing a filter. Resuming an existing conversation preserves its binding. Assigning selected Free-session knowledge to a project does not reclassify the conversation's other contents.

### Explicit sharing

Sharing publishes an operator-reviewed snapshot into a destination scope, with an internal origin link. It does not expose restricted source titles, transcript contents, neighboring records, or original evidence access. Future source edits require publication again. Withdrawing a publication stops future retrieval but cannot remove information already returned to an agent.

The snapshot's destination visibility is governed by the same binding checks. Internal provenance links do not grant source access. The lifecycle ticket owns publication status/update/withdrawal mechanics; this resolution fixes the visibility contract.

### Source provenance and evidence availability

Every new memory write has source attribution, including explicit writes. Fields unavailable from the source remain explicitly unknown; they are never fabricated.

| Attribution | Required meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Source-run identity | Stable service-assigned identity, retained when provisional provenance is later verified. |
| Binding | Bound boundary and project (project absent for Free sessions), plus applicable repository/worktree/session restrictions at the time of the write. |
| Origin | Registered client installation, provider, and internal conversation identity. |
| Agent details | Role/model when known; absence is explicit. |
| Timing and method | Write creation time, observation time when known, and explicit-write or capture method. |
| Native evidence | Provider-native session ID, native event/turn locator, and original transcript locator when available; preserve original-provider attribution. |
| Code evidence | Registered repository and available commit, path, and symbol pointers; no raw source mirror. |
| Verification and availability | Distinguish provisional/verified identity from readable, unavailable, or ambiguous evidence. |

Native provider IDs and data-directory paths are installation-qualified aliases, not globally unique conversation identities. Explicit memory writes may proceed with provisional local provenance before native session verification; later verification adds mappings while preserving the original source-run identity.

Resuming a verified native session on its registered installation retains its conversation identity and creates new source runs for new work. A different provider or an unverified copied/imported session remains distinct until explicitly linked. Capture replay/idempotency and independent-evidence rules belong to their existing capture and lifecycle tickets.

Closing Chartr preserves attribution. Original transcripts may remain accessible only on their originating machine; remote transcript delivery is not required. Missing or ambiguous source evidence is reported visibly, and does not by itself change record eligibility or acceptance. Provider stores remain transcript authorities; SurrealDB does not become a full transcript archive.

### Scope/filter acceptance matrix

These cases determine scope eligibility; the lifecycle ticket separately determines which statuses are eligible. Tests must exercise both explicit access and capture-derived records where applicable.

| Record and requesting session | Scope eligibility |
| --- | --- |
| Project-wide record, same project and boundary on another machine/provider | Include. |
| Eligible operator-wide preference, allowed for the current boundary | Include by default; caller may narrow it away. |
| Repository-specific record, same project and same registered repository | Include. |
| Repository-specific record, another repository in the same project | Exclude unless explicitly shared/generalized. |
| Worktree-specific record, another worktree or clone of the same repository | Exclude unless explicitly shared/generalized. |
| Unrelated project with an identical basename or slug | Exclude. |
| Work record requested from personal, including project/global matches | Exclude unless a destination-authorized publication exists. |
| Private record in the correct project and boundary | Exclude until operator enables private access for the binding. |
| Free-session non-global record | Only the owning session until explicit assignment/publication. |
| Free session seeking project records inferred only from cwd | Exclude. |
| Direct record ID, graph neighbor, or evidence reference outside the binding | Exclude without exposing restricted record content or metadata. |
| Missing/ambiguous source transcript for otherwise eligible knowledge | Include eligible knowledge with evidence unavailable/ambiguous. |
| Legacy record with unmapped project/boundary/sensitivity | Exclude from ordinary agent retrieval pending explicit compatibility mapping. |

Filters compose conjunctively: allowed work/personal boundary and private access, then project or eligible global preference (or the Free session's own records), then every applicable repository, worktree, and session restriction. The global alternative cannot bypass narrower restrictions. A destination publication is eligible only through its authorized destination scope.

Identity acceptance also covers a verified rename, a second-machine clone, a fork requiring linking, duplicate installation/native session identifiers, a resumed conversation, and a fresh conversation after a project/boundary switch. Neither provider changes nor restarted clients widen access.

### Baseline changes and remaining ticket ownership

- Draft sections 6.1, 7.2, and 13's T3-project/basename mapping are replaced by stable memory-project and registered repository/checkout identities. Reason: cross-machine continuity, rename safety, and collision isolation.
- Draft section 6.1's caller-selected sensitivity filters and default `normal,work` behavior are replaced by operator-bound work/personal separation plus private opt-in. Section 11's direct-get filter bypass cannot bypass scope. Reason: agent parameters and record IDs must not expand authority.
- Draft D5 and section 7.1's T3 thread/turn pointers are replaced with provider-neutral, installation-qualified source attribution. D5's no-full-transcript-mirror principle is retained. Reason: Chartr owns conversations/terminal sessions while provider stores own transcripts; there is no assumed T3 turn stream.
- Draft D2's single existing namespace/database is retained; logical boundaries do not require separate databases. D4's source-code pointers and git authority are retained.
- The initial single-machine premise was already superseded by [Choose the first-version provider and rollout contract](03-first-version-support-contract.md); this ticket applies that decision rather than reopening deployment scope.

[Set the knowledge lifecycle and authority rules](05-knowledge-lifecycle-contract.md) owns publication lifecycle, scoped record conflicts, and acceptance/independence rules. [Choose the memory runtime and agent tool boundary](06-runtime-and-tool-boundary.md) owns trusted binding delivery, credential/configuration ownership, concrete schemas, and identity registration mechanisms. [Define automatic capture and extraction semantics](07-automatic-capture-contract.md) owns run granularity, replay, and provider-specific attribution adapters. [Choose retrieval, embedding, and context budgets](08-retrieval-and-embedding-contract.md) applies the matrix to all retrieval paths. [Find the minimal operator memory controls](09-operator-memory-controls.md) owns the binding/link/share interaction. [Define compatibility with existing SurrealDB history](13-existing-surrealdb-history.md) maps existing records without silently assigning scope. These are already-ticketed decisions; no additional fog patch needs a duplicate ticket.

   - Use only project knowledge unless broader recall is requested.
   - Choose separately for each project.

## Baseline corrections and verified facts

- The ticket's single-machine wording is corrected to match the resolved provider/rollout contract. This is not a new scope expansion.
- The selected stable memory-project identity replaces the draft's path/basename-derived project assumption. The selected work/personal boundary requires more than the draft's caller-selected sensitivity filter; round two selects an operator-controlled binding enforced on all access paths.
- Chartr folder-space keys are path based (`crates/chartr/src/space.rs`); foreground cwd is presentation metadata, not ownership. The established UI space model does not itself provide cross-machine memory identity.
- Current conversation keys qualify native session IDs by provider and local data namespace (`crates/chartr-conversations/src/store.rs`). Grok uses `local:grok`; these keys lack a host discriminator. Source identities must not be assumed globally unique.
- Provider stores own transcripts. Durable source pointers and universal cross-client access to source contents are different requirements.

## Round two: answered

The operator selected every recommended answer below. Stable identity linking, project membership, worktree qualification, Free-session behavior, operator-controlled scope, and local-only evidence availability were agreed in this round; the remaining edge cases were settled in round three.

4. **Linking another checkout:** On a second machine, should an exact match to a previously linked repository automatically reuse its memory project?
   - Automatically reuse an unambiguous registered repository identity inside the selected memory boundary; ask for ambiguous matches and forks. Never match solely by basename or path (recommended).
   - Require confirmation for each new checkout, including exact matches.
   - Require manual selection for every new checkout, with no repository-based matching.
5. **Project membership:** Can a memory project contain several repositories or non-git folders?
   - Yes, explicitly link them; keep repository-specific knowledge qualified to its repository (recommended).
   - One repository per memory project; non-git folders get separate projects.
6. **Worktree knowledge:** Should linked worktrees share project knowledge while checkout-specific facts remain local to that worktree?
   - Yes; share project knowledge, keep worktree-specific facts local unless deliberately generalized (recommended).
   - Share all knowledge across the project's worktrees by default.
   - Isolate worktree memory unless explicitly shared.
7. **Free sessions:** What memory should a session without an assigned project access?
   - Select a work/personal boundary and receive its eligible global preferences; keep new non-global knowledge session-local until assigned to a project. Changing cwd does not silently change its memory binding (recommended).
   - Require assigning a memory project before any memory access.
   - Infer the memory project from the current directory and change it when cwd changes.
8. **Scope authority:** May an agent broaden access by passing another project or boundary to a memory tool?
   - No; Chartr's operator-selected binding constrains all reads/writes, direct record lookup, and linked evidence. Agents may narrow scope or request an explicit operator-approved switch/share (recommended).
   - Let agents search all projects within the selected boundary, but require operator approval to cross work/personal boundaries.
9. **Evidence availability:** Must original transcript contents be accessible from every client, or is durable attribution with a visible unavailable-source state sufficient?
   - Durable provider/source attribution is required; evidence may remain readable only on the originating machine. Closing Chartr retains attribution; absent logs are reported as unavailable (recommended).
   - Require original evidence to be readable from every client, adding a remote evidence-access requirement without storing full transcripts in memory.

## Round three: answered

The operator answered "All recommended" to this final round, confirming the proposed scope/provenance contract and its scope/filter examples. Lifecycle status, knowledge deduplication, capture replay, runtime credentials, and legacy-data mapping remain owned by their existing tickets.

10. **Stable identifiers and collisions:** Use opaque, stable identifiers for memory projects, repositories, client installations, checkouts/worktrees, conversations, and source runs. Names, absolute paths, and normalized repository remotes are aliases or locators, never sole durable identities. A registered repository alias may select a project only when unique within the selected boundary. A renamed/moved checkout retains identity when its registration can be verified; otherwise ask to relink. New clones get their own checkout identity while sharing the registered repository/project. Forks, conflicting aliases, duplicate installation registrations, and ambiguous matches never silently merge. Identical knowledge slugs in different projects/boundaries remain distinct; within-scope write conflict policy belongs to the lifecycle ticket.
    - Adopt these identity/collision rules (recommended).
    - Use a different identity or automatic-merge policy, to be specified by the operator.
11. **Meaning of private:** Treat private as an additional opt-in restriction within either work or personal, not as a synonym for personal. Private records are excluded from default recall, bootstrap, direct lookup, and graph/evidence traversal until the operator explicitly enables private access for that binding. Unknown or unmapped scope never becomes global or normal by inference; exact legacy mapping belongs to the existing-history compatibility ticket.
    - Adopt private opt-in and exclusion of unknown scope (recommended).
    - Do not add a separate private restriction; work/personal separation is enough.
12. **Changing scope during a conversation:** Previously retrieved text cannot be removed from a provider's context merely by changing a filter. Switching project or work/personal boundary therefore starts a fresh provider conversation with the new binding. Reusing an existing conversation preserves its old binding; moving a UI pane or changing cwd does not authorize new memory access. Explicit assignment/sharing can move selected Free-session knowledge into a project, but does not silently reclassify that session's existing contents.
    - Start a fresh conversation when changing project/boundary (recommended).
    - Allow an explicit in-conversation scope switch and accept that prior context may be carried into the destination scope.
13. **Explicit sharing:** Share a selected record through a destination-scoped publication linked internally to its origin. The operator reviews the content being exposed; hidden source text, restricted titles, neighboring records, and transcript access do not become shared implicitly. The publication is a snapshot, so future source edits are not published automatically. Withdrawing it stops future memory retrieval but cannot erase content already returned to an agent. Exact publication lifecycle is for the lifecycle ticket; this ticket fixes the visibility requirement.
    - Share reviewed snapshots with destination-specific visibility (recommended).
    - Share the live record so future source updates automatically appear at the destination.
14. **Source provenance:** Every new memory write carries a service-assigned source-run identity and the bound project/boundary, originating installation, provider, conversation, agent role/model when known, creation/observation time, and capture method. Keep native provider session ID, native event/turn locator, original transcript locator, and code pointers (repository plus commit/path/symbol) when available; missing fields are explicitly unknown, never fabricated. Explicit writes without a verified native session may use provisional local provenance; later verification adds a mapping while preserving the original run identity. A resumed verified native session on its registered installation stays the same conversation with new source runs; a different provider or an unverified imported/copied session remains distinct until explicitly linked. Missing transcripts affect evidence availability, not record visibility or acceptance by themselves. Capture replay/idempotency remains for the capture ticket.
    - Adopt this provenance contract, including provisional explicit writes and visible missing evidence (recommended).
    - Block memory writes until a native provider session and exact source location are verified.

# Set the knowledge lifecycle and authority rules

## Question

Which parts of the draft's closed ontology, default statuses, immutable-live-body rule, supersession, reclassification, and confirmation policy should become the Chartr contract? Resolve the tension between explicit human confirmation and promotion after a second provider asserts a slug; distinguish independent evidence from an agent repeating retrieved memory. Decide deterministic update/idempotency behavior, concurrent writes, stale facts, and entity/edge invariants. Audit the draft's conflicting live-status descriptions, unsupported supersession cases, and example edges. Record a reason for each reopened baseline decision.

Apply [Define memory scope and provenance identities](04-scope-and-provenance-identity.md), including its scoped-identity and memory-publication contract. Set publication status, update, and withdrawal mechanics without reopening the agreed visibility rules.

Options for discussion (not decisions):

- Require explicit human confirmation for hard rules; agents may propose and attach evidence
- Allow narrowly defined independent corroboration to activate hard rules
- Retain the draft's second-provider activation rule with explicit safeguards

## Done when

The human agrees to a complete lifecycle/authority matrix, update and conflict invariants, closed vocabulary corrections, and examples that distinguish capture from accepted knowledge.

## Answer

Confirmed by the operator on 2026-09-26. [Discussion history](../assets/knowledge-lifecycle-discussion.md) records the choices and baseline changes.

### Authority and visibility

| Knowledge | Initial state | Ordinary agent access | Transition to instruction authority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Decision | `proposed` | Excluded | Operator accepts it. |
| Constraint and operator preference | `proposed` | Excluded | Operator explicitly confirms it; another provider's assertion only adds evidence. |
| Convention | `proposed` | Excluded | Operator activates it. |
| Skill | `draft` | Excluded from ordinary instructions | Operator activates it. |
| Fact | `asserted` | Eligible with source and validity labels | No rule authority; a fact cannot masquerade as a constraint. |
| Lesson | `active` | Eligible with source and lesson label | Advisory learning, not a hard rule. |
| Incident | `open` | Eligible with source and incident state | `mitigated` or `closed` requires observed evidence or operator confirmation. |
| Concept | `active` | Eligible as a named idea/tag | No rule authority. |
| Thought | `inbox` | Excluded by default | Reclassification creates a typed target under that type's normal authority. |
| Schema proposal | `proposed` | Excluded by default | Operator accepts the proposal; `shipped` additionally requires evidence of a migrated schema. |
| Episode and topology | `open` for an episode; trusted registration for identities | Scope-filtered according to type | Episode status follows source work; identity registration follows the trusted binding contract. |

Ordinary bootstrap and recall exclude `proposed`, `draft`, `inbox`, rejected, withdrawn, expired, and superseded records. An explicitly requested proposal/history view may return them, always labeled and scoped. Direct record lookup does not bypass those access checks. Numeric confidence, another provider, and repeated exposure never confer acceptance. The extraction path may produce observations, facts, lessons, thoughts, and proposals, but capture itself never accepts a decision or activates an instruction.

### Record identity, revision, and replacement

A knowledge key is its trusted home scope plus closed type and writer-controlled slug. The home scope includes the work/personal boundary and the applicable memory project or Free-session identity, with repository/worktree qualifications when the claim is that narrow. A slug or path alone cannot merge records across scopes. A destination publication is a separate scoped record, not a second home for its source.

Every semantic mutation has a monotonic server revision and audit entry with actor/source run, time, previous revision, and reason when meaning or authority changes. Proposed/draft text may be intentionally amended through a revision-checked edit with the same audit trail; a conflicting `remember` call does not count as such an edit. On accepted or otherwise active knowledge, a strictly cosmetic typo correction may revise in place; changing meaning, scope, or authority creates a new key and a `supersedes` lineage edge. The old record becomes terminal `superseded` and leaves ordinary retrieval. Add `superseded` to every replaceable semantic type, including decision, constraint, convention, lesson, incident, skill, preference, fact, concept, and episode; keep their other type-specific states. Rejected and withdrawn records remain historical. An old record has at most one direct successor. A successor may replace several old records. A split marks the old item `superseded` with a split reason and links the new items as related outcomes without claiming a single direct successor.

The edge direction remains `successor ->supersedes-> predecessor`. The invariant is at most one incoming `supersedes` edge per predecessor, not one outgoing edge per successor as the draft says. A `supersedes` edge requires compatible type and authorized scope, an existing predecessor, an existing successor, and a terminal predecessor state; no cycles. The new record, old status, and lineage edge commit together. A split has no `supersedes` edge; its reason and related-outcome links commit with the terminal status instead.

An identical retried operation on a scoped key returns its prior result. â€œIdenticalâ€ means the same canonical operation and input fields, not a model's judgment that two texts mean the same thing. Independently observed evidence is attached as a separate, provenance-bearing assertion. A different body, scope, status intent, or authority on the same key returns a conflict requiring an explicit successor or a new slug. Every body, status, scope, or successor mutation checks an expected server revision; a losing concurrent writer receives a revision conflict and must re-read before deciding. Status and edge updates are atomic. Idempotency keys protect delivery retries, while source-run attribution and capture fingerprints are specified by the capture ticket.

### Evidence, validity, and thought promotion

An evidence assertion records whether its source run independently observed the claim or derived it from retrieved memory. Different providers alone do not establish independence. Derived repetitions may be retained as provenance but do not count as corroboration. They never activate a hard rule. Evidence pointers remain access-controlled and may report the original source as unavailable without changing an eligible record's status.

Facts have inclusive `valid_from` and exclusive `valid_until` only when supported by the source or an explicit operator decision. There is no invented 90-day default. An expired fact leaves ordinary retrieval and remains in history. Conflicting current facts retain both claims, carry a contradiction link and visible conflict label, and are presented together for review when retrieved; a newer timestamp or higher confidence does not silently choose a winner. A source correction uses supersession, not an unrecorded overwrite.

Reclassifying a thought keeps the original as provenance and creates or identifies one current typed target. The target receives its type's default state and acceptance policy. Promotion does not widen the thought's trusted scope without operator review, and an existing same-key target still follows the conflict rule. The thought's `promoted` state and `promoted_to` edge commit with the target. A failed transaction leaves the thought unpromoted. Reclassification does not invent a new node or edge type.

### Publication and graph invariants

A publication starts as a draft destination-scoped snapshot and becomes active only after the operator reviews its visible content and destination. Source edits never update it implicitly. A changed snapshot or destination requires a new reviewed version; activation supersedes the previous published version atomically. Withdrawal changes an active publication to terminal `withdrawn`, stopping future retrieval while preserving audit history. An internal origin link does not grant access to the source record, source title, evidence, or neighbors. Publication cannot bypass work/personal, private, repository, or worktree binding rules.

Node and edge types remain closed. Unfitted content becomes a `thought`; an agent may suggest a schema proposal, but only a deliberate schema decision can accept it and only a migration can ship it. The draft's automatic â€œfive similar thoughtsâ€ proposal trigger is removed. Every graph edge must have existing endpoints, a permitted typed direction, and a scope check on creation and traversal. Relations do not confer access to a restricted endpoint. Duplicate edge operations are idempotent where the relation is unique; repeated evidence assertions retain their own provenance. The draft's `decision ->constrains-> interface` example is invalid for its declared edge types: link the decision with `affects`, or create an actual constraint before using `constrains`.

### Baseline corrections and acceptance examples

- Draft D3 and the closed vocabulary remain. D11's agent-created schema-proposal similarity trigger is dropped because it can manufacture taxonomy pressure from repeated or derived content; a human schema decision remains required.
- Draft D7's second-provider activation path is removed because provider diversity does not establish authority or independent evidence. Explicit operator confirmation controls constraints and preferences. Convention and skill activation follows the same instruction-authority principle.
- Draft D9's writer-controlled slug remains, but its identity is qualified by trusted scope; otherwise identical slugs across projects or boundaries collide. Its upsert rule becomes exact idempotent retry plus explicit conflict and supersession.
- Draft section 9's proposed-as-live list is corrected to exclude proposals from ordinary retrieval, matching the selected visibility rule. Draft sections 10.4 and 8 gain cross-type supersession states and the corrected edge cardinality. Draft section 10.1's cosmetic-edit exception becomes an audited revision with a narrow definition.
- Agent A captures â€œnever use raw `/dev/mem`â€ as a proposed constraint. Agent B reads and repeats it: the repetition is derived evidence; neither agent activates it. It enters normal bootstrap only after operator confirmation.
- Two agents independently record the same dated fact: the first fact stays asserted, and the second source is independent evidence. If they assert conflicting current values, recall shows both with a conflict marker. A source-grounded expiry removes an old value from ordinary recall without deleting it.
- An accepted decision changes scope from one worktree to its memory project: create a reviewed successor with a new key, atomically supersede the old decision, and do not let the old record's evidence or links widen access by inheritance.
- Two writers attempt different successors of the same decision: one atomic revision-checked transition wins; the other receives a revision conflict. An exact replay of the winner returns its recorded result.

# Define historical session import semantics

## Question

How should v1 derive typed semantic memories from pre-existing Codex, Claude Code, and Grok sessions on macOS/Linux while retaining provider transcripts as the source of record? Given the provider/rollout contract and common ingestion semantics, decide session discovery and selection, supported historical formats, import provenance and authority, overlap with live capture, stable deduplication, progress and cancellation, checkpoint/restart behavior, incomplete evidence handling, and resource budgets. Distinguish historical session import from adopting a pre-existing semantic memory database. Do not silently drop Grok or turn SurrealDB into a transcript archive.

Options for discussion (not decisions):

- Feed historical sessions through a common capture/extraction contract with import-specific discovery and checkpoints.
- Use a dedicated batch-import pipeline with an explicit compatibility boundary to live capture.

## Done when

The human agrees to import scope, compatibility/error reporting, provenance and authority invariants, replay/deduplication semantics, operational controls, and acceptance examples for every required provider. Create bounded research or prototype tickets for unresolved factual or behavioral questions rather than guessing.

## Ruled out

The operator clarified that historical access means reusing the already-running SurrealDB instance and its stored memories/history. Separate import of older provider sessions not already stored there is not required in v1. This ticket was opened from an overly broad interpretation of "old sessions" and sits beyond the clarified destination. Existing-history compatibility remains in [Define compatibility with existing SurrealDB history](13-existing-surrealdb-history.md); new-work extraction remains in [Define automatic capture and extraction semantics](07-automatic-capture-contract.md).

# Define compatibility with existing SurrealDB history

## Question

How should Chartr use the operator's already-running SurrealDB instance and make its stored history available without losing provenance, changing existing meanings, or disrupting current consumers? First establish read-only evidence of the actual database/namespace, schema, record lifecycle and scope conventions, and what stored history means. Then decide compatible read/write boundaries, identity and scope mapping, representation of records outside the draft's vocabulary, coexistence with current clients, and whether any explicit migration or adapter is necessary. Reusing the existing instance/history is a requirement; provisioning an unrelated fresh database is not an equivalent outcome. Distinguish database history access from importing older provider transcript files.

Options for discussion (not decisions):

- Reuse existing schema/contracts directly wherever compatible, with narrow adapters for differences.
- Maintain an explicitly mapped Chartr representation in the existing instance while retaining access to original history and current consumers.

## Done when

The human agrees to a compatibility and coexistence contract grounded in the actual existing data model, with explicit history-access acceptance examples and any migration prerequisites separately ticketed. Do not treat a failed harness-memory adapter as proof that SurrealDB is unavailable; do not guess schema or alter the database during discovery.

fog.title: Provider-specific exceptions
fog.body: Capability research and the selected support matrix may expose incompatible identity, capture, or MCP behaviors. The concrete exceptions needing their own decisions are not yet known; revisit after provider support and capture are chosen.

fog.title: Quality and performance experiments
fog.body: The retrieval and extraction contracts may need empirical calibration against representative operator work. Workloads, failure thresholds, and the experiments that could change a decision are not yet established.

fog.title: Cross-contract gaps
fog.body: Reconcile the final ontology, capture, runtime, confirmation, and recovery choices. New questions may emerge from their interaction; graduate only those that can be stated precisely.

exclusions.title: Production implementation
exclusions.body: Building and shipping the memory service, database migrations, provider wiring, and UI is outside this planning map.
exclusions.reason: The agreed destination is an implementation-ready design; throwaway research and prototypes only support decisions.

exclusions.title: Multiple operators and replicated memory
exclusions.body: Team ACLs, multi-tenant hosting, replicated databases, and mobile synchronization are excluded. One operator connecting macOS/Linux clients to the same existing Windows-hosted database is in scope.
exclusions.reason: The operator requires reuse of one existing instance across these client platforms; replication and multiple operators are not required.

exclusions.title: Full memory browsing and editing
exclusions.body: A general memory explorer, graph editor, and comprehensive editing UI are excluded.
exclusions.reason: The user selected minimal setup, health, and confirmation controls.

exclusions.title: Replacing source and conversation stores
exclusions.body: Replacing git or provider transcript stores, rewriting Chartr's terminal UI, storing raw source/full transcripts in SurrealDB, and building a full code graph are excluded.
exclusions.reason: These are baseline non-goals and are unnecessary for shared semantic memory.

exclusions.title: Automatic ontology expansion and formal reasoning
exclusions.body: Agent-created tables/edge types, OWL/SHACL reasoning, and multi-embedder indexing are excluded.
exclusions.reason: Preserves the draft's bounded first-version model; reopening requires a recorded scope decision.

exclusions.title: Native Windows support
exclusions.body: Native Windows support is deferred from the first-version memory contract.
exclusions.reason: The operator selected macOS and Linux.

exclusions.title: Define historical session import semantics
exclusions.body: Separate import of older provider transcript files is outside v1. Closed tracker ticket: .plan/maps/chartr-agent-memory/tickets/12-historical-session-import.md.
exclusions.reason: The operator clarified that historical access means the memories/history already stored in the existing SurrealDB instance.
